Reporting with Tracksuit
A practical framework for communicating brand health – building reporting rhythms that connect your data to your goals, so the right people see the right story at the right time.

Good brand reporting isn't about sharing data - it's about connecting brand health to what the business is trying to do.

That means starting with the business or marketing goal, not the dashboard. Are you trying to grow the top of funnel? Defend a perception position? Understand how a campaign moved the needle? The goal shapes which metrics matter, which time window to use, and how much competitive context your audience needs.

Start with the goal
What is the business or marketing team trying to achieve right now? Let the answer define what you report on.
One story per slide
The best reports make one clear point, well. A board update isn't a summary of every metric - it's the most important finding, in context.
Always end with so what
Data without implication is noise. Every report should answer: what does this mean for what we do next?
Context setting
What Impacts Brand Health Metrics

Brands do not operate in a vacuum. Brand health is shaped by a mix of factors, some in our control, many not. Spend does not always equal growth (sadly).

When reviewing Tracksuit data, we encourage you to zoom out and ask the right questions to unpack what drivers are at play. It is normally many at once compounding together, and this is why context really matters.

Quick reference when reporting with Tracksuit
Which view should I use?
→
Funnel overview
A point-in-time snapshot. Use when you want to show where your brand sits right now, including funnel size, conversion rates, and competitive position.
Best for
Setting the scene
Snapshot of market position
Establishing a baseline
↗
Trend line
Movement over time. Use when you want to show whether a metric is growing, declining, or holding, and whether that change is sustained.
Best for
Post-campaign reads
Mid-funnel drift or recovery
Spotting early momentum
⇄
Period comparison
Two windows, side by side. Use when you want to show a specific change: this quarter vs last, or before vs after a campaign or investment.
Best for
Quarterly or bi-annual reviews
Proving campaign ROI
Year-on-year storytelling
Which time window should I use?
3 months
Most recent · pulse check
The default for funnel metrics. Gives you the latest read with enough sample size for reliable results in most categories.
Use for
Awareness, consideration, usage, preference
Quarterly reporting cycles
Campaign impact checks
Not recommended for statements or small segments.
6 months
Balanced · best for perception data
The right window for statements, imagery, and segment cuts. More statistical stability, especially when you're looking at sub-groups or attribute scores.
Use for
Statements and imagery
Demographic or segment cuts
Bi-annual reviews
Good middle ground between recency and reliability.
12 months
Long view · sustained direction
Best for annual storytelling or when you want to smooth out seasonal spikes and show the underlying brand direction over a full year.
Use for
Annual brand health reviews
Year-on-year comparisons
Categories with strong seasonality
Shows whether you're growing vs riding the same seasonal wave every year.

Thought starters
Audience
Which audience matters most to the business right now? Total market, or a specific segment?
Performance
What does your key metric look like for that audience? And how has it moved?
Is the change you're seeing statistically meaningful?
What's happened that could explain this movement? (e.g. campaign, pricing, distribution, PR)
Competitive context
Is this result isolated to your brand? Your key competitor? Or is the whole category moving in that direction?
What next
Does this result mean we stay the course, adjust, or escalate?

How to measure in the dashboard
Statements Overview Statements Comparison Imagery
Prompted attributes Top of mind associations
Pair with
Statements + Double IndexingTraining Ground + Imagery
→ How your brand performs on each attribute (Statements), which attributes you distinctively own vs brand size (Double Indexing), and what people say unprompted (Imagery), the full perception picture
Statements + Imagery
→ Are the associations you're strongest on in Statements showing up unprompted in Imagery? When they do, it's a signal those attributes are genuinely embedded in memory, not just recognised when prompted.
Statements + Advanced conversion driversTraining Ground
→ Understand which statements have the greatest importance in driving conversion at the top and bottom of the funnel, so you can focus your efforts where they'll have the most impact.
Thought starters
Performance
Where in the funnel is the business focusing their efforts? What does statement performance look like for this metric? Does this differ for the total market vs priority segments?
Competitive context
Is a competitor gaining on an attribute you own? Are you defending your position? Have you seen improvements when comparing statements over time?
Memory structures
Are the important attributes already top of mind and showing in the Imagery tab? What differentiates you from a competitor and what advantage does that give you?
What next
Do perception results mean we stay the course, adjust, or escalate?
Before you interpret
Run these sense checks before drawing conclusions from your data.
?
Does your category experience strong seasonality?
If yes, a single quarter's read may reflect the time of year more than brand performance. Use a longer window or compare the same period year-on-year.
?
Were there any survey or methodology changes over the period?
Changes to survey structure or data collection can create artificial shifts in metrics. If something looks unusual, check with your Brand Champion before drawing conclusions.
?
Are you focusing on the wrong part of the funnel?
If awareness is low (e.g. 10%), focus on building awareness before looking further down the funnel. Does your narrative align with where the business actually is?
